common_name: Water Pepper (Smartweed, Tade, Marsh Pepper Knotweed)

planting.note: Direct sow into consistently moist to boggy soil after frost danger passes; it thrives at pond margins, in rain gardens, or in a container standing in a saucer of water, and self-sows freely once established.

directions: Sow seed shallowly into wet, rich soil or shallow standing water in full sun, thinning seedlings once established; the plant self-sows readily, so many gardeners simply let a small patch persist year to year. Young leaves and sprouts carry a sharp, peppery bite from a compound related to capsaicin and are used fresh in Japanese cuisine, most famously as benitade, the tiny red-leaved sprouts served with sashimi, and historically as a pungent seasoning across Europe before black pepper became widely available. Harvest leaves continually through summer for the strongest heat and pinch flower spikes to keep foliage production going. Because it spreads by seed in wet ground, site it where naturalizing is welcome rather than near sensitive wetlands.

planting.note: Best established from root divisions or nursery plugs set into permanently damp, mineral-rich soil; it spreads by thick aromatic rhizomes and colonizes wet seeps, ditch banks, and pond edges.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions into saturated, mineral-rich soil in full sun to light shade near a pond edge, rain garden low point, or irrigated bed that never fully dries out. The thick, spicy-scented roots have long been used by Southwestern Indigenous peoples and traditional herbalists as an antimicrobial wash and poultice, and the plant is equally valued as a striking wetland groundcover with white, cone-centered spring flowers reminiscent of anemones. It spreads steadily by rhizome once established, so give it room or a contained wet bed. Divide congested clumps in early spring to renew vigor and share starts.

planting.note: Best fall-sown or cold-moist stratified for 60 days, since seed benefits from winter chilling; established plants are long-lived and need little further attention.

directions: Sow stratified seed or set out plugs in prairie or meadow plantings with well-drained to average soil; the smooth, glaucous, silver-backed leaves make a bold textural statement even before the flat-topped clusters of small ivory flowers open in mid to late summer. It is a favorite nectar source for a wide range of small bees, wasps, and beetles, and its architectural height and pale foliage pair well with grasses and taller composites in a naturalistic border. Once established the deep taproot makes the plant very drought tolerant and it rarely needs staking despite its height. Leave seed heads standing through winter for visual interest and to let it self-sow modestly.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or cold-moist stratify 60-90 days before a spring sowing; it resents transplanting once its taproot is established.

directions: Direct sow into well-drained prairie soil, dry-mesic meadow plantings, or gravelly slopes where competition is low, since it establishes a deep taproot early and does not transplant well. In its second year it sends up flat yellow umbels in mid-spring, among the earliest umbellifer blooms available to emerging native bees and small pollinators. As a true prairie relict it tolerates drought and poor soil once established but is intolerant of heavy, wet clay. Let seed heads mature and shatter naturally to maintain a self-sustaining population, since it is a short-lived perennial that relies on some recruitment from seed.

subcategory: prairie and glade native pollinator annual

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring onto bare, well-drained soil, since seed needs light to germinate and should not be buried deeply; it also self-sows readily once established in a bed.

directions: Scatter seed onto lightly raked, well-drained soil in a sunny rock garden, glade planting, or short-grass prairie mix and press in without covering, since germination is light-dependent. The small white-to-pale-lavender, yellow-centered daisies resemble a miniature aster and bloom heavily from mid-spring into early summer, attracting small native bees and syrphid flies. It behaves as a short-lived annual or biennial in most gardens, persisting through reseeding rather than by rootstock, so avoid mulching too heavily over the seedbed. It is well suited to lean, rocky, or sandy soils where more aggressive perennials would crowd it out.

planting.note: Fall-sow or cold-moist stratify 30-60 days before spring sowing; established plants spread slowly by rhizome and are best left undisturbed once sited.

directions: Plant in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun, where its distinctive basal rosette of leaves and nearly leafless flowering stalks distinguish it from the taller, leafier sunflowers most gardeners already grow. Bright yellow, 2 to 3 inch composite flowers open from late summer into fall on wiry stems, providing a valuable late-season nectar and pollen source for bees and butterflies as many earlier bloomers fade. It is notably drought tolerant and thrives in poor, sandy, or rocky soils where richer ground would cause it to flop or be outcompeted. Divide clumps every few years if they become congested, and avoid overly fertile or irrigated beds, which promote lanky growth.

common_name: Upland White Goldenrod (Prairie Goldenrod, White Aster-Goldenrod)

planting.note: Fall-sow onto well-drained, lean soil or cold-moist stratify 30-60 days before spring sowing; it establishes best in gravelly or rocky prairie-type ground rather than rich garden beds.

directions: Grow in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil such as limestone glades or gravelly prairie plantings, since this unusual goldenrod bears flat-topped clusters of white, aster-like ray flowers rather than the typical yellow plumes of its relatives, a trait that once led botanists to classify it as an aster. It blooms in late summer and fall, complementing true asters and providing a valuable pale counterpoint to yellow prairie goldenrods while still attracting the same broad range of native bees, wasps, and butterflies. Unlike many goldenrods it stays compact and well-behaved, spreading slowly rather than aggressively colonizing by rhizome. It performs best where soil stays on the dry, mineral side and struggles in rich, moisture-retentive garden loam.
